item.research_question: How can thermo-mechanical processing (TMP), specifically rolling and subsequent annealing, be tuned to achieve superior strength–ductility synergy in single-phase and multiphase high entropy alloys (HEAs) at room temperature?
item.material_system: Single-phase FCC (e.g., CoCrFeNiMo0.15, CoCrFeNiMn, CoCrFeMnNi, Al0.25CoCrFeNi), single-phase BCC (e.g., HfZrTiTaNb), single-phase B2 (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1), and multiphase alloys (e.g., FCC+BCC, FCC+HCP, L12+B2)
item.processing_route: Thermo-mechanical processing (TMP) involving rolling (cryo-rolling, room-temperature rolling, warm rolling, hot rolling) followed by annealing; parameters include rolling temperature, total plastic strain, strain path (unidirectional vs. cross rolling), symmetricity (symmetric vs. asymmetric rolling), annealing temperature, annealing time, and heating rate.
item.test_conditions: Room temperature tensile testing to evaluate yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, ductility, and the strength–ductility synergy parameter (PSD in GPa × %); hardness testing for HPT processed samples.
key_findings: Cryo-rolled (CR) specimens exhibited more strengthening than room-temperature rolled (RTR) specimens due to higher dislocation density, intersection of twins, TRIP, and more shear banding.
Asymmetric rolling (ASR) strengthened the FCC CoCrFeMnNi alloy by 96% more compared to symmetric rolling (SR) due to higher dislocation density and intersecting twins.
The strength–ductility synergy (PSD) of RHPed HEA reached a maximum of 60 GPa × % (FeCoCrNiMn-1 at % C), comparable to TWIP steel (58 GPa × %) and TRIP steel (51 GPa × %).
The highest yield strength of RHPed HEA reached 1437 MPa (AlCoCrFeNi2.1), close to Fe-20 Cr-20 Ni steel (1428 MPa).
HPT combined with thermal annealing imparted a 400% increase in hardness to Al0.3CoCrFeNi HEA.
High heating rates during annealing achieved lower grain sizes and better yield strength compared to low heating rates (0.013 °C/s).
The recrystallization activation energy in FCC HEA (549 kJ/mol) is significantly higher than in high manganese steel (230 kJ/mol) and TWIP steel (229 kJ/mol).
Addition of 2 atom % titanium in CoCrFeMnNi alloy followed by HPT showed 830% total elongation at 700 °C due to a grain size of 30 nm.
item.mechanism: Strengthening is driven by dislocation activity, grain refinement, deformation twinning, shear band formation, and back stress hardening during rolling. Annealing optimizes properties through recovery, recrystallization, and precipitation, where precipitates inhibit grain growth and sluggish diffusion delays recrystallization kinetics. The synergy is enhanced by heterogeneous microstructures generated via hybrid rolling (e.g., cryo + warm) and intersecting twins from asymmetric rolling.
item.limitations: The text notes that as-synthesized HEAs have inherent limitations such as gas porosity, shrinkage porosity, and un-melted particles which create inhomogeneous stress distribution. Additionally, excessive grain growth at high annealing temperatures can deteriorate strength, and the recrystallization kinetics in HEA are slower than in conventional alloys due to sluggish diffusion and lattice distortion.
item.future_work: The authors propose using hybrid rolling (combination of cryo-rolling and warm rolling, symmetric and asymmetric rolling) to generate hierarchical heterostructures. They suggest employing Integrated Computational Materials Engineering (ICME) to predict processing–property correlations and reduce experimental needs. They also recommend microstructure and crystallographic texture simulations and the use of SPD techniques like accumulative roll bonding to develop multilayers with hierarchical microstructures.
quotes: The strength–ductility synergy is quantified as a product of strength and ductility (PSD in GPa × %) defined elsewhere.
The best strength ductility combination (PSD) of RHPed HEA (maximum PSD of 60 GPa × % FeCoCrNiMn-1 at % C) is in the same range of TWIP steel (PSD: 58 GPa × %).
